entity_title: Employer must register with ESD first
fact_text: A relocating professional cannot apply for a Malaysian Employment Pass themselves. The hiring company must first register with, and be approved by, the Immigration Department's Expatriate Services Division (ESD) before it can submit any expatriate pass application.
evidence_quote: All companies will need to register with the ESD as a first step.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the employee applies for their own Malaysian work visa. Actually the employer must first register and be approved with the ESD before any Employment Pass can be lodged. Action: confirm your employer already holds an active ESD account before agreeing a start date.

fact_text: Before a company can register with ESD to sponsor expatriates it must meet two requirements: incorporation with the Companies Commission of Malaysia (SSM) and a minimum paid-up capital - RM250,000 for a 100% local-owned company, RM350,000 for a joint venture (minimum 30% foreign equity), or RM500,000 for a 100% foreign-owned company.
evidence_quote: There are two requirements needed before companies can proceed with the ESD registration.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed any registered employer can sponsor a foreign hire. Actually the sponsoring company must clear a minimum paid-up-capital threshold (up to RM500,000 for a 100% foreign-owned entity) before ESD registration. Action: check that a newly incorporated or thinly capitalised employer can actually meet the capital gate.

entity_title: ESD company registration takes 14 working days
fact_text: Once complete documents are submitted, ESD company registration takes 14 working days. Because the employer must be registered before it can lodge an Employment Pass, this lead time sits before the individual's pass processing even begins.
evidence_quote: it takes fourteen (14) working days for the process to be completed.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a work pass is issued within days of accepting an offer. Actually, if the employer is not yet ESD-registered, that registration alone takes 14 working days before any Employment Pass can be submitted. Action: ask whether the employer is already ESD-registered, or add 14+ working days up front.

entity_title: Director must sign Letter of Undertaking in person
fact_text: To activate its ESD account the company Director must attend in person to sign the Letter of Undertaking (LoU); no one may represent the Director. Until activation is complete the employer cannot submit expatriate applications.
evidence_quote: A company Director has to be present for the submission of the LoU.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed immigration onboarding can be fully delegated to HR or an agent. Actually a company Director must appear in person to sign the Letter of Undertaking before the ESD account is activated. Action: schedule the Director's LoU appointment early, as it blocks all pass submissions.

entity_title: EP categories I/II/III and revised salary thresholds
fact_text: The Employment Pass has three categories (I, II and III), each with its own minimum monthly salary threshold. A revised Employment Pass Salary Policy took effect on 1 June 2026, updating the minimum salary thresholds and adding a structured employment duration framework.
evidence_quote: updates to the minimum salary thresholds for Employment Pass (EP) Categories I, II, and III, as well as a structured employment duration framework.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed there is a single flat salary rule for a work visa. Actually eligibility depends on which of three EP categories the role falls into, and the thresholds were revised from 1 June 2026. Action: confirm the offered salary meets the current threshold for the intended EP category.

entity_title: Category I EP requires RM20,000 and above
fact_text: Under the revised policy, Employment Pass Category I covers strategic positions and critical expertise and applies to salaries of RM20,000 and above per month.
evidence_quote: Category I salaries of RM20,000 and above

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a single modest salary threshold qualifies any expatriate. Actually the top tier, Category I (strategic and critical roles), applies to salaries of RM20,000 and above. Action: map the role to the correct EP category before assuming which salary threshold applies.

entity_title: EP tied to a local-talent replacement plan
fact_text: The revised policy requires employers to prepare a replacement plan to train local employees to take over the expatriate's role within the employment period. If an employer fails to implement the replacement plan, its future expatriate applications may be affected or rejected.
evidence_quote: Future applications may be affected or rejected.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed an Employment Pass renews automatically as long as the job continues. Actually renewals and future applications depend on the employer implementing a local-talent replacement plan. Action: understand the employer's replacement-plan commitments, as they can affect your ability to extend.

entity_title: Dependants are not automatic under the EP
fact_text: Bringing dependants to Malaysia is not automatic under an Employment Pass. It is subject to meeting salary eligibility, insurance coverage requirements and immigration regulations, with dependants covered by a separate Dependant Pass sponsored by the employer.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed family members are automatically covered once you hold an Employment Pass. Actually dependants need a separate Dependant Pass and are subject to salary-eligibility and insurance requirements. Action: verify your salary meets the dependant threshold and arrange the required insurance before relocating family.

entity_title: Tax residency is 182 days, not nationality
fact_text: Malaysian income-tax residency is determined by physical presence, not nationality or visa type. An individual who is not physically present in Malaysia for at least 182 days in the basis year is generally not a tax resident for that year.
evidence_quote: present in Malaysia for at least 182 days in the basis

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed that holding a long-term work pass makes you a 'resident' for tax. Actually tax residency turns on being physically present at least 182 days in the tax year, independent of immigration status. Action: track your entry and exit days, especially in your arrival year.

entity_title: Non-residents are taxed at a flat 30%
fact_text: Employment income of a non-resident individual is taxed at the non-resident tax rate of 30%, instead of the graduated resident scale rates. In the arrival year a relocating employee is often a non-resident until the 182-day threshold is met.
evidence_quote: at the non-resident tax rate of 30%

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you are taxed at the same progressive rates from day one. Actually, until you qualify as a tax resident (182 days), your Malaysian employment income is taxed at a flat 30%. Action: budget for the higher non-resident rate in your first year and check whether resident status can be recomputed once you cross 182 days.

fact_text: A non-resident individual is not entitled to claim personal relief (nor the rebate available to residents); the resident scale rates and reliefs apply only once the individual qualifies as a Malaysian tax resident.
evidence_quote: Personal Relief Not entitled to claim

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you can claim the usual personal deductions and reliefs immediately. Actually a non-resident is not entitled to claim personal relief or the resident rebate. Action: do not assume relief-reduced tax while you are still a non-resident in your first year.

entity_title: Keep entry/exit records to prove residency
fact_text: To determine tax-residency status by day count, LHDN expects supporting records including a certified true copy of the passport, a list of entries and exits, and departure flight tickets. Retaining these is the individual's responsibility.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the tax office already knows how many days you spent in Malaysia. Actually you may need to prove your day count with a certified passport copy and a list of entries and exits. Action: keep passport stamps, an entry/exit log and flight tickets from your arrival onward.
